title: Where spread can be interrupted: the six links
audience: Cleaning and support workers in healthcare and residential care settings who need to understand why each cleaning or hygiene step exists.
learningOutcomes: Name the linked conditions that must all be present for infection to spread.
Match a worker action to the link in the chain that it breaks.
Explain why the chain can be broken at more than one point and why early action matters.

instruction.heading: Six linked conditions
instruction.body: Infection spreads only when several conditions coincide. An infectious agent must be present. It needs a reservoir where it lives, a way out of that reservoir, a mode of travel, a way into a new person, and a susceptible person who can be infected. Remove any one link and the spread stops. A separate factor, the level of exposure, decides how likely infection becomes once a microbe reaches a person. It depends on the environment, temperature, how many organisms there are, the person immune strength and how many people share the space.

instruction.heading: Reservoirs go well beyond people
instruction.body: Many workers assume the reservoir is always a sick person. In practice a reservoir can be a piece of equipment, blood or other body fluid, food, water, soil and waste, a surface, or a frequently touched place such as a door handle, a light switch or a call bell. Animals and birds can also act as reservoirs. Surfaces and equipment are where cleaning acts on the reservoir, and that is why the cleaning schedule matters even when nobody in the room is unwell.

instruction.heading: Exits and entries are body openings and broken skin
instruction.body: Organisms leave a body through the nose, mouth, the bowel and genital openings, and through broken skin. They enter through the eyes, nose, mouth, bowel and genital openings, and through broken skin. A cut or abrasion is therefore both a possible exit and a possible entry, which is why “Cuts, abrasions and skin conditions at work” deals with covering cuts before any task. The fastest way to break these links is to keep your own breaks in skin covered and to avoid touching your eyes, nose or mouth with contaminated gloves or hands.

instruction.heading: Modes of transmission and the controls that break them
instruction.body: Microbes travel by contact, whether direct with a person or indirect through a surface or object; by droplets from coughs and sneezes; by airborne particles; by vectors such as ticks, mosquitoes, fleas and flies; and by penetrating injury such as a needle stick. Each mode has a matching break. Hand hygiene and gloves break contact spread. Covering coughs and sneezes breaks droplet and airborne spread. Keeping waste sealed and out of reach breaks spread through waste. Tidy, controlled work areas break spread through vectors. Sharps handling breaks the penetrating route, and “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response” covers it. The controls work best together, because no single one is reliable on its own.

procedure: Identify the infection concern for the area from the schedule or from the nurse in charge.
Ask which link you can most easily affect in this task: the agent, the reservoir, the exit, the route of transfer, the entry or the susceptible person.
Choose the control for that link from the schedule or the infection control procedure. Do not invent a new control.
Apply the control in the order the schedule sets, and keep hand hygiene in place throughout.
Record the control you used and the link it addressed, and report any link you could not break.

workedExamples.situation: In a residential aged care home, a cleaner finds a commode with spilled urine beside a resident who has a dressing on a leg wound.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which links are in play, and which one can you break?
workedExamples.reasoning: The urine and the commode are a reservoir. The wound is a possible entry point for organisms. Your hands are the route of transfer. You break the transfer route with gloves, clean the commode by its method, and wash your hands afterwards. You report the wound to the nurse, who manages it.

workedExamples.situation: A visitor coughs repeatedly at the reception desk of a medical clinic while waiting to be seen.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which link does the cough represent, and what do you do?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cough is a portal of exit and a mode of transmission through droplets. You make sure tissues and a no-touch bin are available, point the visitor to hand rub, and tell the reception staff so they can manage the waiting area. You clean the desk surfaces the visitor touched using the approved product.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves for any task involving body fluid or a contaminated surface
Approved hand rub or hand-washing supplies
Cleaning schedule and approved product list for the area

commonErrors.error: Treating a sick person as the only source and ignoring surfaces, equipment and waste.
commonErrors.prevention: Check every reservoir in the area, not only the people in it.

commonErrors.error: Relying on one control and assuming the chain is broken.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the layered controls set by the schedule and procedure together.

commonErrors.error: Waiting until the chain looks complete before acting.
commonErrors.prevention: Act on the first sign of infection, because an early break limits spread.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Where a link involves a wound, a sharp or a body fluid, follow the specific procedure for that hazard. Do not wait for the wider picture to be confirmed.
Choose products from the facility list and the label. Do not select a product because it seems stronger.

qualityStandard: Learner names the six linked conditions in their own words.
Learner matches at least three worker actions to the correct link.
Learner explains why surfaces and equipment count as reservoirs.
documentationEvidence: Log entry with the area, the link addressed, the control used and the time.
Record of any link the worker could not break, with the person it was reported to.
summary: Infection needs all of its linked conditions to be present, so breaking any one link stops spread.
Reservoirs include surfaces, equipment, waste and body fluids, not only people.
Acting early on the first sign of infection breaks the chain more easily.

knowledgeChecks.question: A door handle in a ward has been touched by many people and holds microbes. Which element of the chain does the handle represent?
Which action breaks the link at the mode of transmission?
options: Wiping a bench with a dry cloth only and then leaving it
Hand hygiene between tasks and gloves when handling body fluid
Storing clean linen next to waste in the same cupboard
Leaving a spill until the shift is over and then wiping it quickly

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should an early sign of infection be acted on quickly?
options: The chain can be broken at any point, and an earlier break limits spread
Early signs mean the person is contagious for the rest of the stay
The chain stops working after the first symptom
You should diagnose the infection yourself so the record is accurate
